blocks.text: From what has been said I think it is clear that the חולד choled of Moses was the mole, just like the Syriac ܚܘܠܕܐ chulda and the Arabic خلد [khuld] chuld or chold. Yet it must not be concealed that among the Talmudic doctors חולדה chulda is for the most part the weasel. The following passages make this plain. In the tractate Cholin, cited above: חלדה הר בחלדה הדרה בעיקרי בתים דמכסי הכא, "The thrusting in of the knife in slaughtering is called Chalada, an expression borrowed from chulda, which lives in the foundations of houses so as to lie hidden there." This does not fit the mole, which lives only in the field, but it fits the house-dwelling weasel, κατοικίδιον [katoikidion]. To this is regularly opposed חולדת סנאים or חולדת הסניים, the weasel of the brambles, that is, the wild weasel: as in Kilaim ch. 8, fol. 32. a. b., הקופד וחולדת הסניים, "the hedgehog and the weasel of the brambles." There the Gloss of Maimonides says: וחולדת הסניים חיה דומה לחולדה ממיני השועלים, that is, "The weasel of the brambles is a wild animal similar to the common weasel, among the species of foxes." And in Bava kama ch. 4, fol. 80. 1: מגדלין כלבין כופרין וחתולין וקופין וחולדות סנאים מפני שעושין לנקראת הבית, "One may raise village dogs, and cats, and monkeys, and weasels of the brambles (which are called חולדות), because they are made for digging through houses." And shortly after: אמר ר׳ יהודה שרצא חרצא ואיכא דאמר חרזא דקטני שקי דרעיא ביני וורדיני, "R. Iuda said: It is a creeping thing (CHARTSA) that cuts. And there are those who say (CHARZA) that bores, because it has slender legs and feeds among thickets." So too Pliny, [II, 444] book 29, chapter 4: "There are two kinds of weasels: one is wild. They differ in size. The Greeks call them ictidas, etc. But this one, which roams about in our houses," etc. That the Talmudists generally take חולדה chulda to be the weasel, not the mole, as we have said, also follows from their claim that this animal strangles children, which no one would say of the mole. To this end a passage is cited from the tractate Thaanith ch. 1, fol. 8. 1: בא וראה כמה גדולים בעלי אמנה מניין מחולדה ובור ומה המאמין בחולדה ובור כך המאמין בהקב״ה על אחת כמה וכמה, "Come and see how the chulda and the pit are reckoned among the great witnesses of faith. And who trusts the chulda [col. 1028] and the pit, and would not trust much more the Holy One, Blessed be He?" On this passage the Talmudic Glossator relates this tale: מחולדה ובור שהמיתו שני בני אדם מצוי הוא באגדה מעשה בבחור אחד שנתן אמונתו לריבה אחת שישאנה אמרה מי העיד והיה שם בור א׳ וחולדה אמר הבחור בור וחולדה עדים בדבר לימים עבר על אמונתו ונשא אחרת והוליד שני בנים אחד נפל לבור ומת ואחד נשכתו חולדה ומת אמרה לו אשתו מה מעשה הוא זה שבנינו מתים במיתה משונה ואמר לה כך וכך היה מעשה, "The chulda and the pit, by which two people were put to death. The story is found in the Aggada about a certain young man who pledged his faith to a girl that he would marry her. 'Who will be witness?' she said. Now there were there a pit and a chulda (weasel). And the young man said: 'The pit and the chulda will be witnesses of the matter.' But some days later he broke his pledge and married another, who bore him two sons. One of these fell into the pit and died; the other also died, bitten by a chulda, or weasel. Then, when his wife asked him why both sons had died a violent death, he told her how the matter stood." Baal Aruch relates many more details of the same story, among them that the child was a boy, already three months old, strangled by the chulda. The words are: וילדה בן זכר כשהגיע לג׳ חרשים חנקתו חולדה, "And she bore a male son, whom the chulda strangled when he had already reached the third month." Likewise, of the الزبزب [al-zabzab] zebzeb, a kind of larger weasel or ferret, caught at Baghdad in the year 304 of the Hegira, the Arabs related above^{e)} انه ياكل اطفالهم [annahu yaʾkul aṭfālahum], that it devoured their infants, and bit men's hands and women's breasts. To this must be added what the Talmudists adduce in comparing the words חולדה chulda or חולד choled and חלד cheled. The latter means the world in Ps. XLIX, 2., where men are called יושבי חלד, inhabitants of cheled, that is, of the earthly world. And the doctors dispute among themselves why the earth is called חלד cheled, and ask what it has in common with חולד choled, the animal. In the Babylonian Talmud, tractate Cholin ch. 9, fol. 127. a., someone answers: כל שיש ביבשה יש בים חוץ מן החולדה, "Whatever animal is on land is also in the sea, except only the chulda." Lest this be thought said without grounds, [II, 445] here is a pretty story which the most learned Buxtorf brings from the writings of the Rabbis in his Lexicon Talmudicum under the word חלד: "The princes of the world held an assembly on right government. The prince of the sea complained that he did not have enough subjects. He was therefore permitted to seek more from the land, provided he made provision for their food. He cast all the land animals into the sea, with the command that they should propagate their kind there too. So it was done; hence it is said that all land animals are also in the sea, except that some have been changed into monstrous form. When he came to the weasel, she, standing on the shore, said to the prince of the sea: 'Why will you throw me into the sea again? Do you not see that I am already in the sea?' She said this showing her image in the sea. The prince was satisfied and let the weasel go. Hence the Talmudists say that all land creatures are in the sea except the weasel, which escaped by her cunning. And the earth is called חלד cheled because it remained the property of the weasel, which is called חולדה chulda or חולד choled." In the Jerusalem Talmud, at the beginning of the chapter On the eight creeping things, the same question is treated, and some answer the very thing we have just said, that the earth and earthly men are compared with the chulda: לפי שכל מה שיש ביבשה יש בים והרבה מינין יש [col. 1029] בים מה שאין כן ביבשה ואין חולדה בים, "because, although everything that is on land is also in the sea, and there are many species in the sea that are not on land, yet the chulda is not in the sea." The other answer is this: חולדה זו גוררת ומנחת ואינה וודעת למי מנחת כך כל באי העולם גוררין ומניחין ואינן יודעין למי מניחין כמו שנאמר יצבור ולא ידע מי אספם, "The chulda drags in many things and leaves them behind, not knowing for whom she leaves them. So also all worldly people drag in many things and leave them behind, not knowing for whom they will leave them. As it is said Psal. CXXXIX, 2.: 'He will heap up, and will not know who will gather them'." So the Aruch cites these things, which, however utterly trifling, nevertheless serve our purpose. For they show that by the word chulda most Talmudists do not mean the mole. For the mole, which is blind, would not be said to have seen its image in the sea and shown it to others. Nor is it read to store up and hide anything in its burrows. But this is the disposition of the weasel, of which Abdollatiph of Baghdad writes, in the place cited above: في طبعه انه يسرق ما وجد من فضة او ذهب كما يفعل الغار [fī ṭabʿihi annahu yasriq mā wajada min fiḍḍa aw dhahab kamā yafʿal al-ghār], "It is in its nature to steal whatever silver (or gold) it finds, as mice do." And so in the same place this story is told of the weasel: رجل صاد فرخا منها وحبسه في قفص بحيث تراه امه فلما اراته ذهبت ثم جات وفي فمها دينار فالقته بين يديه كانها تفدي ولدها فلم يتركه لها فذهبت وعادت بدينار اخر حتي بلغت من العدد خمسا فلما [II, 446] ان لا يطلق لها ذهبت وعادت بخرقة كانها تشير الي فراغ حاصلها فلم يكترث بها فلما رات ذلك عادت الي دينار فاخذته منه فخشي الرجل من ذلك فاطلق لها ولدها [rajul ṣāda farkhan minhā wa-ḥabasahu fī qafaṣ bi-ḥaythu tarāhu ummuhu fa-lammā arāthu dhahabat thumma jāʾat wa-fī famihā dīnār fa-alqathu bayna yadayhi kaʾannahā tafdī waladahā fa-lam yatrukhu lahā fa-dhahabat wa-ʿādat bi-dīnār ākhar ḥattā balaghat min al-ʿadad khamsan fa-lammā an lā yuṭliq lahā dhahabat wa-ʿādat bi-khirqa kaʾannahā tushīr ilā farāgh ḥāṣilihā fa-lam yaktarith bihā fa-lammā raʾat dhālika ʿādat ilā dīnār fa-akhadhathu minhu fa-khashiya al-rajul min dhālika fa-aṭlaqa lahā waladahā] "A certain man caught a weasel's young and shut it in a cage, so that the mother could see it. When she had seen it, she went away and came back with a denarius in her mouth, which she threw down before him, as though to ransom her young. But when he did not release it, she went off again and brought more denarii, until she reached the number five. And when she saw that her young was still not released, she also brought a cloth (in which the coins had been), to show that she had exhausted her whole store. And when she noticed that no heed was paid to her, she went back to the coins to take them back. But the man, struck with fear, returned her young to her." It is clear, then, that by the word חולדה chulda the Talmudists mostly mean the weasel. But their authority in this matter moves us little, since they are not consistent with themselves, and among the Arabs and Syrians chuld [col. 1030] or chulda is the mole; and both the origin of the word and the circumstances of the Mosaic text plainly show that the word is to be taken in this way.
